title: Typing Functions
summary: A function type describes its inputs and the kind of answer it returns.
introduction: A function type describes its inputs and the kind of answer it returns. Label the numbers going into a small maths helper. Then label the answer, so the checker can catch a text value used in the wrong place.
learningObjectives: Annotate parameters and return types and read the errors for wrong or missing arguments
Declare optional, default and rest parameters in the right order
Describe callbacks with function type aliases and rely on contextual typing

blocks.text: Parameters are the one place where inference cannot help: the compiler has no way to know what a caller will pass, so under `strict` every parameter needs a type. The return type can usually be inferred from the `return` statements, but annotating it on anything exported turns the signature into a contract that the body cannot accidentally break. Arrow functions are typed the same way.

blocks.title: basics.ts
npx tsc basics.ts
blocks.content:
basics.ts:8:1 - error TS2554: Expected 2 arguments, but got 1.

8 add(1);
  ~~~

  basics.ts:1:25
    1 function add(a: number, b: number): number {
                              ~~~~~~~~~
    An argument for 'b' was not provided.


Found 1 error in basics.ts:8

blocks.text: Running the file with `tsx` prints `5 42`; in plain JavaScript the call `add(1)` would silently return `NaN`. The compiler instead reports the call *and* points back at the parameter that was not provided. Argument count is checked as strictly as argument type: passing too many arguments is also an error, which catches a whole family of copy-and-paste mistakes.

A question mark makes a parameter optional; inside the function its type gains `| undefined`, so you must handle the missing case. A default value (`greeting = "Hello"`) also makes the parameter optional, but the type is inferred from the default and never includes `undefined` inside the body. A rest parameter collects any number of trailing arguments into an array.

blocks.title: params.ts

blocks.text: Note the `??` operator: `punctuation ?? "!"` uses the default only when `punctuation` is `null` or `undefined`, which is exactly the case the `?` introduced. Inside `sum`, `values` is a `number[]`, so the arrow function passed to `reduce` gets `total` and `value` typed as numbers without any annotation.

blocks.title: Common mistake: an optional parameter before a required one
blocks.text: `function slice(start?: number, end: number)` is rejected with `TS1016: A required parameter cannot follow an optional parameter.` Callers fill parameters left to right, so there would be no way to supply `end` without `start`. Put optional and default parameters last, or accept a single options object when a function has several optional settings.

A function is a value, so it has a type: the parameter list and the return type written with an arrow, such as `(value: number) => string`. Giving that type a name with `type` makes it reusable. When you pass an arrow function where a function type is expected, the compiler *contextually types* its parameters from the expected signature, so `(value) => ...` needs no annotation and still gets full checking.

blocks.title: callbacks.ts
npx tsc callbacks.ts
blocks.content:
callbacks.ts:10:39 - error TS2322: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.

10 console.log(formatAll([3], (value) => value * 2));
                                         ~~~~~~~~~

  callbacks.ts:1:18
    1 type Formatter = (value: number) => string;
                       ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    The expected type comes from the return type of this signature.


Found 1 error in callbacks.ts:10

blocks.text: The first call prints `[ '1.50 EUR', '20.00 EUR' ]`. The second is rejected because the callback returns a number where `Formatter` promises a string, and the message tells you which signature imposed the expectation. This is the same mechanism that types the callbacks you pass to `map`, `filter`, `addEventListener` and every library API.

`void` says a function's return value is not meant to be used; `logLine` below returns nothing, and callers that try to use its result get an error. `never` says the function does not return at all: it throws or loops forever. The compiler uses that knowledge for control flow: after `fail(...)` is called inside the `if`, it knows the code below only runs when `port` is a real number.

blocks.title: void-never.ts
npx tsx void-never.ts (Node prints the stack trace after the message)
blocks.content:
> port 8080
Error: Not a port: abc

rows: Always returns a value of that type
Functions that always throw; exhaustiveness checks

blocks.title: Overloads and generics
blocks.text: Sometimes one function accepts several unrelated shapes, such as `parse(text: string)` and `parse(bytes: Uint8Array)`. TypeScript supports *overload signatures* for that, but the more common tool is a generic function, which the [generics lesson](/tutorials/typescript/generics) covers. Reach for overloads only when the return type genuinely depends on which parameter shape was used.

questions.question: Inside `function tag(label?: string) { ... }`, what is the type of `label`?
questions.explanation: An optional parameter may be omitted, so inside the body its type is the declared type plus undefined. You must handle that case before calling string methods.

questions.question: An arrow function passed to `[1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2)` needs an explicit `n: number` annotation under strict mode.
questions.explanation: The parameter is contextually typed from the array's map signature, so n is already a number. Annotations are only required where no context exists.

seo.title: Typing Functions in TypeScript – Parameters and Returns
seo.description: Learn to type function parameters, return values, optional and rest parameters, callbacks with function types, and the void and never return types.
